title: When you stop, and start again
hook: two weeks of all five, then one missed, then none: the deeds most loved are the steady ones, even if small

segments.voice: Yesterday: fajr, the whole dawn prayer, every piece in order, takbir to taslim. Your line was the whole thing. Today, what happens after you've learned it, and then stop. Day one hundred thirteen.

It happens so often it barely needs telling. Ramadan, or a new year, or a hard week, and the prayers come back. Two weeks, all five. Then one gets missed. Then two. Then the adhan sounds from a phone across the room, there's a sting of guilt, and the prayer still doesn't happen. A few months later, the whole thing starts again. Underneath sits one quiet question: am I a bad Muslim? Today, what the tradition says to someone stuck in that loop.
screen: `TWO WEEKS, ALL FIVE.` → `THEN ONE MISSED. THEN NONE.` → `AM I A BAD MUSLIM?`

segments.voice: First, the plain part, said once. Across the major schools, the five daily prayers are a duty, not an extra. This lesson doesn't soften that. It's about how people actually get back to them. Aisha, the Prophet's wife, reported a saying that speaks straight to the loop. The Prophet ﷺ was asked which deeds are most loved by Allah. The most constant ones, he said, even if small. In Arabic, wa in qall: even if it is little. And she added that when he began something, he kept it up. Notice what's being praised. Not the heroic week. The thing that keeps going. That's why many teachers, when someone has drifted, don't say all five tomorrow or don't bother. They say: pray the next one. Guard it. Then add another. The goal stays five; the way back is one at a time. If there's a long stretch of missed prayers behind you, scholars differ on how to make them up, so that's a question for a teacher you trust, not a reason to wait. Then there's the voice that says you've already failed. Camp two gave it a name: waswas, the whisper. One of its oldest tricks is telling a person the door has shut. A saying the Prophet reported from Allah, in Bukhari, says the opposite: whoever draws near to Me by a hand's span, I draw near by an arm's length; whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running. And it's fine to ask for help with the praying itself. The Prophet told the companion Mu'adh that he loved him, then taught him to say at the end of every prayer: O Allah, help me to remember You, to thank You, and to worship You well.
screen: `THE DUTY IS FIVE, PLAINLY.` · `MOST LOVED: THE STEADY ONES, EVEN IF SMALL.` · `PRAY THE NEXT ONE. GUARD IT. ADD ONE.` · `COME WALKING, AND HE COMES RUNNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit comfortably, and breathe. If you pray, choose just the next prayer, the one that's coming, and decide only that one. Not the whole week. If you've been away for a while, picture yourself making wudu for it, and let that be enough for now. If you don't pray, choose one small good thing you once kept up and let slide, and picture doing it once more. Breathe out the guilt. Breathe in the next one. The bell holds the time.
Wa in qall. Even if it is little: from the saying that the deeds Allah loves most are the most constant ones, even if small. Today's word.
Your line: small, steady, and back again. The goal stays five, and the way back starts with the next one. Day one hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Muslims hold the five daily prayers to be a duty; when someone has drifted from them, many imams and teachers advise coming back prayer by prayer, keeping each one steady, and asking a trusted scholar about making up what was missed.

fork.setup: you've missed a week of prayers. the next adhan sounds, and a voice says: you've already blown it, why bother? what does today's lesson point to?
options: wait until you can do all five perfectly
pray the next one, and guard it
fork.reveal: pray the next one. the deeds most loved are the steady ones, even if small, and the goal stays five.

original.note: Arabic: even if it is little, from the saying adwamuha wa in qall, the most constant of them, even if small.

trapdoor: what you thought: once you've stopped praying, you've failed, so why start again?
what it means: wa in qall — the steady deeds are the most loved, even if small; the way back is the next prayer.

what a scholar hears: adwamuha wa in qall (Bukhari 6464, Muslim 783); the hadith qudsi of the hand's span and the running (Bukhari 7405); Mu'adh's du'a at the end of every prayer (Abu Dawud 1522); qada', where the schools differ.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 6464 (the most beloved deeds to Allah are the most constant, even if small)
Sahih Muslim 783 (Aisha: when he did a deed, he kept it up)
Sahih al-Bukhari 7405 (hadith qudsi: a hand's span, an arm's length; walking, running)
Sunan Abi Dawud 1522 (Mu'adh: O Allah, help me to remember You, thank You and worship You well)
Qur'an 4:103 (prayer prescribed for believers at fixed times)

NEW lesson from the map's #1 change (the pray-stop-restart cycle, the most repeated r/islam theme: REDDIT.md #5; REDDIT_REPLIES.md §6; THREADS_AND_COMMENTS.md §5). It replaces 'The fingers will testify' (Tirmidhi 3583, counting on the fingertips); that content now lives as one line in day 114, and the post-prayer count is still taught on days 114 and 116.

Sensitive (gradualism vs obligation, REDDIT_REPLIES.md §6d): the script states the duty plainly first ('the five daily prayers are a duty, not an extra') and presents 'pray the next one, then add' as how many teachers advise coming back, with 'the goal stays five'. Please confirm the balance reads right.

It deliberately doesn't rule on the status of someone who has stopped praying (the schools differ, and a Hanbali position is severe) or on how to make up years of missed prayers (qada'); it sends that question to a trusted teacher.
Hadith numbers cited from memory; please confirm: Bukhari 6464 / Muslim 783 (adwamuha wa in qall), Bukhari 7405 (hadith qudsi), Abu Dawud 1522 (Mu'adh, 'la tada'anna fi dubur kulli salah').
'Across the major schools' for the five prayers being obligatory: the four Sunni schools and the Ja'fari school; confirm the wording.
